1281.quote_or_event: “All the rest of the world is deluded by doubt, while my mind is intoxicated with the Sublime Essence of the Lord.”
1281.explanation: Kabir says his mind is drunk not on any worldly drink but on the sweet essence of the Lord.
1281.tie_back: The Kural says love, not wine, can delight a person merely by thinking of or seeing the beloved; Kabir likewise speaks of an intoxication that comes from love of the Lord rather than from drink.
1281.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 92, Sri Raag, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1281._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; a good fit on love as an intoxication greater than wine, though Kabir's intoxication is spiritual (the Lord's essence) and the Kural's point about thinking and seeing is not explicit.

1282.quote_or_event: “Don't be angry - drink in the Ambrosial Nectar; you shall not remain in this world forever.”
1282.explanation: Guru Nanak tells the listener to give up anger and drink in the nectar of the Name, because life is short.
1282.tie_back: The Kural says that when love is as tall as a palm tree one should not sulk even a millet-grain's worth; Guru Nanak likewise counsels dropping anger in favour of the sweetness of love while there is time.
1282.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 931, Raag Raamkalee, Dakhni Oankar, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1282._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; next-best match: both advise giving up anger for the sake of love, but the Kural's playful lovers' sulk (ūṭal) is not the moral anger (krodh) that Guru Nanak warns against.

1283.quote_or_event: “Even if You cut my body apart, I shall not pull my limbs away from You.”
1283.explanation: Kabir declares that whatever the Lord does to him, even cutting his body apart, he will not turn away.
1283.tie_back: The wife in the Kural says that even if her husband neglects her and does as he pleases, her eyes cannot rest without seeing him; Kabir likewise vows a love that does not turn away whatever the beloved does.
1283.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 484, Raag Aasaa, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1283._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; a strong fit on love that endures the beloved's harshness, though Kabir's devotion is to God and his image is far more extreme than the Kural's neglect.

1284.quote_or_event: “The bumble bee becomes enticed by the lotus, intoxicated by its fragrance, and does not leave it, even for a moment.”
1284.explanation: Guru Arjan pictures the devotee drawn to the Lord as a bee is drawn to the lotus, unable to leave it.
1284.tie_back: In the Kural the wife set out to sulk, but her heart forgot and went straight to union; Guru Arjan's bee likewise cannot hold back from the lotus that draws it.
1284.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 454, Raag Aasaa, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1284._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; next-best match: both show a heart irresistibly drawn to the beloved, but the Kural's comic forgetting of a planned sulk is absent; the love is spiritual.

1285.quote_or_event: “He covers the faults of His servant.”
1285.explanation: In the Sukhmani, Guru Arjan says the Lord hides and overlooks the faults of His devotee.
1285.tie_back: The Kural's wife cannot see her husband's faults when she sees him, as the eye cannot see the kohl brush; Guru Arjan's line, in reverse, has the Beloved overlooking the devotee's faults.
1285.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 285, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1285._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; next-best match only: love overlooking faults is shared, but here it is the Lord who covers the devotee's faults, the reverse of the Kural, and the kohl-brush simile has no parallel.

1286.quote_or_event: “They complain about other peoples' faults, while their own self-conceit only increases.”
1286.explanation: Guru Ram Das warns that those who keep finding fault in others only feed their own ego.
1286.tie_back: The Kural's wife sees nothing but her husband's faults when he is away, and none when he is present; Guru Ram Das likewise shows that fault-finding grows when the heart is cut off from love and ego takes over.
1286.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 366, Raag Aasaa, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1286._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; next-best match only: it concerns fault-finding, but as a moral warning about ego (haumai), not the Kural's tender observation that absence makes faults loom large.

1287.quote_or_event: “The storm rages and the rain floods the land; thousands of waves rise and surge.”
1287.explanation: In these extra saloks Guru Nanak pictures a world of storm and flood, in which the seeker must hold on to the Lord.
1287.tie_back: The Kural compares useless sulking to leaping into a flood one knows will sweep one away; Guru Nanak's line shares the image of an overwhelming flood.
1287.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1410, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1287._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; weak, next-best match: only the flood image is shared; the Kural's point that sulking is futile when one knows love will win has no real Sikh parallel, and only this single line is quoted.

1288.quote_or_event: “Even if You give me hunger, I will still feel satisfied; I am joyful, even in the midst of sorrow.”
1288.explanation: Guru Ram Das says that whatever the Beloved gives, even hunger and sorrow, he accepts with joy.
1288.tie_back: The Kural's wife says her husband's embrace still draws her like drink draws the drinker, even though it brings her pain; Guru Ram Das likewise clings to the Beloved even when it brings hardship.
1288.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 757, Raag Soohee, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1288._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; next-best match: both accept pain for the sake of the beloved, but the Kural's craving like a drinker for wine (and its playful 'thief') has no parallel, and Gurbani elsewhere condemns intoxicants.

1289.quote_or_event: “The path they take is sharper than a two-edged sword, and finer than a hair.”
1289.explanation: In the Anand Sahib Guru Amar Das says the way of the devotees is so fine and demanding that few can walk it.
1289.tie_back: The Kural says love is more delicate than a flower and few grasp its finest moment; Guru Amar Das likewise says the path of love for God is finer than a hair and walked by few.
1289.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 918, Raag Raamkalee, Anand Sahib (pauri 14), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1289._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; reasonable but partial: both describe love's path as exceedingly fine and rarely mastered, but Guru Amar Das stresses its sharpness and difficulty rather than the Kural's softness and delicacy; the love is spiritual.

1290.quote_or_event: “The Gurmukhs are honored in the Court of the Lord. The Lord Himself takes them in His Loving Embrace.”
1290.explanation: Guru Ram Das says the Lord Himself draws those who follow the Guru into His loving embrace.
1290.tie_back: The Kural's husband recalls how his wife, after a brief sulk with her eyes, melted into his arms more eagerly than he; Guru Ram Das likewise ends in the Beloved's loving embrace.
1290.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 42, Sri Raag, Guru Ram Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
1290._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via BaniDB (Sant Singh Khalsa translation) on 2026-10-10; next-best match: the loving embrace is shared, but the Kural's sulk-then-surrender is absent, and in Gurbani it is the Lord who embraces the devotee; the love is spiritual, not romantic.
